title: Specs Powell, Sticks Evans and Billy Gladstone at Radio City
summary: Jones tells how he kept Specs Powell in the drum chair and advised him and Sticks Evans to be percussionists, linking them to Radio City's Billy Gladstone.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: J. C. joined Cab, I remember.

He joined Cab. Cozy went to CBS. Now after Cozy stayed there for a while, then they had this big show coming along. The war's going on now. They had this big show coming along. Now me and Sidney said, "Who can we get to play in Cozy's place with Raymond Scott?" That's when we went and got Specs Powell. Specs was leaving for 6 months, he was leaving every night. We'd get him down on 52nd Street and say, "If you leave we'll throw you off the Brooklyn Bridge. You have to stay." He said, "Why don't you all come down and play?" We said, "No, you stay. You are a percussionist. You are a musician. I knew you as a piano player, a vibraphone player, you stay."
Well, I got news for you. He finally left in '73. He's retired. He was the longest musician to stay there...
Right. A tremendous musician, a tremendous percussionist.

I said, don't worry about it. The worst thing that John Hammond could ever do - I got him with Eddie South down at Cafe Society and he played "The Sheik of Araby" and the Down Beat said, "He's going to be the successor of Jo Jones." I said, "No, never. You're a percussionist; you don't know how to play no jazz. You know more music than the musicians you're going to play with. You just stick with the drums, write your xylophone parts, write your vibraphone parts, write your chime parts, He said 'yes, but -' I said, and you just stay right there. "Go to Minton's or somewhere and jam and get it out of your system. I'd love to have a boom-ch, oom-ch, oom-ch-boom job with Guy Lombardo and make a million dollars a year and just go out and get me some kicks." You know, Specs was a musician; he was a percussionist. That's why I made Sticks Evans - I said, "You will not -"
Sticks Evans is another percussionist, young percussionist.

I said, "You will not - you are a percussionist." The first time he ran to me and said, "Guess what?" I said, "What are you talking about?" Before he could open his mouth I said, "You're going to play Radio City." He said, "How do you know?" I said, "They're friends of mine." Naturally I was hanging out with Mr. Billy Gladstone and the people at Radio City - that's Wall Street and Mr. Billy Gladstone would

sit and look and hear guys play and he already knew he was the epitome. He was such a flexible man, you see. He knew the peoples that I knew from living in Washington - he knew the Johnsons, he knew the peoples. That's the reason he could understand me. I knew the Chick Webbs and Sid Catletts and what have you, but to know these peoples and to have that background, you see. It was something different, Milt.
